transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-29
Time: 10:00 AM - 10:45 AM ET
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Rivera (Redwood SE), Mark Reynolds (Aurora Bank), Priya Kapoor (Aurora Bank), Daniel Hsu (Aurora SRE)

Summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on latency tuning. Reviewed Time-to-first-token (TTFT) numbers, streaming behavior, sequence length tradeoffs, and kernel choices. Action items assigned for benchmarks and kernel notes; follow-up scheduled.

Topics: TTFT variance, streaming vs non-streaming, batching & seq length, kernel selection (fp16 vs int8), KV cache behavior, fallback strategies, next steps for pilot expansion.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, happy holidays and thanks for making time. Quick check, can you hear me all OK?
[00:05] Mark: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Sofia.
[00:08] Priya: Yep, good here.
[00:10] Sofia: Great. Today's a quick 45 to go over the latest numbers we sent, focus on TTFT, streaming, and the kernel choices Ethan's been testing. Ethan, do you want to start with the high-level perf summary?
[00:25] Ethan: Yeah, sure. So we ran three sets of runs last week — baseline hosted run, Dedicated-style reserved pool sim, and then a dev on-prem-ish run approximating your infra. The headline: TTFT is the biggest variance source, especially when we go from cold to warm KV cache. Cold requests for seq len 1024 are around 780 to 980 ms TTFT depending on kernel, while warm cached ones drop to ~120-180 ms.
[00:45] Mark: Wait, 780 to 980 ms, is that with streaming disabled?
[00:50] Ethan: Good catch — the 780 to 980 was non-streaming full generation turnaround. When we enable streaming the first token latency improves, TTFT drops to ~420-520 ms for cold, and warm streaming first token is around 80-120 ms.
[01:10] Daniel: Do you mean first byte or first token? We saw some noise in our measurements where network jitter shows up as first-byte latency.
[01:16] Ethan: We measured TTFT as first token emission from the runtime, so that should be fairly consistent. There is some variability on the network side — your dev cluster reported small packet drops during one run which probably inflated a subset.
[01:28] Priya: Can you remind me which model variant these numbers were on? We had been testing the rwd-large-8k-quant model? (pronunciation off)
[01:35] Ethan: Right, it's the rwd-large-8k-int8 variant — quantized int8 kernels. We did a compare across fp16 kernels and int8. FP16 gave slightly better cold TTFT in some cases because the kernel startup overhead is smaller, but int8 gives much better sustained throughput and cost.
[01:52] Mark: Huh, I thought int8 startup overhead would be lower since there's smaller memory footprint?
[01:56] Ethan: It's a bit nuanced — some int8 kernels require additional dequantization steps or use fallback slow paths for certain attention ops depending on sequence length. So the runtime ends up doing a bit more orchestration on cold start. Once warmed, int8 is superior.
[02:12] Sofia: OK. Let's talk about sequence length — you mentioned 512 vs 1024. What was the tradeoff?
[02:18] Ethan: At seq len 512, overall TTFT cold is ~460-620 ms non-streaming, warm ~90-140 ms. At 1024 non-streaming cold is the 780-980 ms range I said earlier. So doubling seq len increased the first-token cost substantially because of kernel tiled matmuls and KV cache sizing. Streaming helps but doesn't eliminate the increase.
[02:38] Mark: For our use case — short customer support queries — 512 is probably fine, but for some longer-context fraud detections we need 1024. Can we dynamically route?
[02:46] Ethan: Yes, our routing policy can shard by seq length or latency tier; one pattern is to route short requests to an fp16 low-latency pool and long ones to an int8 high-throughput pool. There's a small model variant compatibility surface we check at runtime, but it's feasible.
[02:59] Priya: That routing adds complexity for us though — we want predictable SLOs.
[03:03] Sofia: Predictability is exactly why we recommended a dedicated pool for the heavy workloads. That gets you steady TTFT and reduces cold noise. We can still do per-path routing but keep the pools dedicated.
[03:13] Mark: Can you quantify how much Dedicated reduced cold TTFT noise?
[03:17] Ethan: In our dedicated sim, where GPUs are warmed and we pinned kernels, cold TTFT max dropped from ~980 ms to ~620 ms for 1024 non-streaming; warm stayed similar. The variance tightened - 95th percentile came down by ~30%.
[03:29] Daniel: Did you test with our estimated QPS? We expect bursts to 40 qps with batching windows of 20-30 ms.
[03:35] Ethan: Yup, we ran burst tests at 40 qps. Under those burst patterns, batching helps throughput, but it does add to TTFT for non-streaming since we wait for the batch. Streaming reduces perceived latency since the first token comes earlier even if batch completes later.
[03:51] Mark: So we should tune batching and streaming together. Any recommended values?
[03:55] Ethan: For your profile I'd suggest aggressive streaming with batch window 15-20 ms for short queries, and 30-40 ms for long seq runs. Also enable prefix KV caching for repeated customer prompts — that moved median by ~50 ms in our runs.
[04:08] Priya: About KV cache — do we need to explicitly manage eviction or does Redwood handle?
[04:12] Ethan: The runtime handles KV cache heuristics automatically but we expose TTL and pinning controls. For high-reuse prefixes we recommend pinning; for ephemeral contexts use conservative TTL so memory stays bounded.
[04:22] Priya: Okay. Can you talk a little about the kernel choices — you mentioned some kernels fell back for attention patterns?
[04:28] Ethan: Right — for certain sequence lengths and layer dims, the int8 path uses a fused attention kernel that isn't stable across all dims, so we have a fallback to a reference kernel (still int8 but slower), which explains some cold spikes. We're working on a patched kernel that covers those dims; I can share the bench notes.
[04:42] Mark: Is that patched kernel something we'd have to ship in our private deploy?
[04:46] Ethan: If you go private/on-prem, yes we'd coordinate a kernel update as part of the runtime package. For Hosted/Dedicated we push updates server-side.
[04:53] Daniel: Any security implications for kernel updates? Our auto-approval for infra changes is slow.
[04:58] Sofia: We'll treat kernel updates like normal runtime releases — release notes, sig checks, and we can provide a tarball with hashes for your security team. Priya, that matches your internal process?
[05:09] Priya: Yes, that helps. We'll need a short security brief.
[05:13] Sofia: We'll include that in the docs we send.
[05:16] Ethan: Also, one more note — TTFT measurements differ between first-token streaming vs first-byte because of the tokenizer step. If you run the tokenization client-side and pass bpe ids directly, you can shave off ~25-40 ms consistently.
[05:28] Mark: We can try client-side tokenization for latency-critical paths. Is there a sample client you can share?
[05:33] Ethan: Yep, I'll include a snippet.
[05:35] Sofia: Great. Let's surface recent numbers you got last Thursday — on the spreadsheet we saw a run labeled "dev-2026-12-23-a"
